Beyond this, they can also be used to obtain traffic counts and classify vehicles using object detection models such as You-Only-Look-Once (YOLO) (Zhang, Liang, and Wang 2025). However, they also have a significant drawback: during inclement weather and at night, their detection is a lot less reliable due to a decrease in image quality (Kaur et al. 2023). • Radar sensorsare widely used for traffic on land, in the air, and on the water. They support tracking and rout- ing of vessels, especially in air traffic and marine traffic, where routes are less constrained by physical features. In road traffic, radar sensors are used for traffic counts, occupancy, and speed monitoring. Depending on the model and configuration, they can differentiate different vehicle sizes and lanes. This data is traditionally used to understand longer-term traffic patterns, but as real-time sensor access emerges, they can be used to support traffic control (Wang et al. 2022), autonomous vehicles (Xu, Yuan, et al. 2023), or perform real-time analysis and prediction tasks, such as crash detection (Moriano et al. 2024). • Light Detection and Ranging (Lidar)sensors are traditionally less commonly used in transportation, but their capability to obtain 3-dimensional data makes them invaluable for (semi-)autonomous vehicles on the road and in the air (unmanned aerial vehicles). • Toll systemsare placed along express lanes or entire highways, and they have largely replaced staffed toll booths. They collect vehicle data (license plate number or transponders) and charge drivers according to their road use. Some toll systems operate for all vehicles whereas others may only track and charge freight vehicles or vehicles using express lanes. • Loop detectors(Mid-Atlantic Entry Systems Virginia 2015) are placed in the roads at signalized intersections. They serve as inputs for traffic signal controllers, letting them know when vehicles are present. Some loop detectors have trouble detecting smaller traffic participants such as bicyclists. Furthermore, when a loop detector breaks, the only way to replace it is to dig up the road, which is expensive, time-consuming, and unpleasant for traffic participants. • Camera-based detectorsare increasingly replacing loop detectors as they are less expensive to install, easier to replace and maintain, and much more customizable than a loop detector. A single camera can detect ve- hicles in a large number of lanes using virtual detectors, as long as it has a good view of the road. Using the camera data, it could be possible to implement prioritization for specific types of vehicles (e.g. buses). De- pending on the model of camera and software, these detectors can detect lane occupancy, vehicle turn counts, speeds, and other traffic data. Like CCTV cameras, these detectors are affected by light and weather conditions (Shao et al. 2022). • Bluetooth-based travel time systemsuse roadside sensors to capture the Media Access Control (MAC) addresses from Bluetooth devices on the passing vehicles and the associated timestamp.
